pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 📊 **Strand 4 — Handling Data**
Collecting, organising, presenting and interpreting information to make good decisions.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B7.4.2)
- B7.4.2.1 — Identify the sample space for a probability experiment involving a single event and express the probabilities of given events as fractions, decimals, percentages and/or ratios to solve problems.

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- describe events as impossible, possible or certain
- classify outcomes of probability experiments (coins, dice) by their likelihood
- list the sample space of an experiment
- calculate probabilities and express them as fractions, decimals, percentages and ratios

pages.title: The language of chance
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Demonstrate understanding of the likelihood of a single outcome occurring by providing examples of events that are impossible, possible or certain from personal contexts.
Curriculum indicator B7.4.2.1.1
[[fig:m7-f74|Figure 15.1: The probability scale]]
> 🔑 **Key idea: Likelihood** — An event is **impossible** if it can never happen (probability 0). It is **certain** if it must happen (probability 1). Otherwise it is **possible** — it may or may not happen (probability between 0 and 1). Possible events can be described as unlikely, even chance or likely.
## ✏️ Example 15.1
Describe each outcome using impossible, possible or certain.
a) A dog will fly tomorrow. b) Someone in your class will become a teacher in the future. c) Ghana will still be an African country tomorrow.
**Solution**
a) **impossible** b) **possible** c) **certain**
## ✏️ Example 15.2
In groups, discuss each event using impossible, possible or certain.
A. A coin lands heads side up. B. The day after Monday will be Tuesday. C. A new-born baby will be a girl. D. It will rain in Winneba in the first week of January.
**Solution**
A. **possible** (an even chance) B. **certain** C. **possible** (about an even chance) D. **possible** (but unlikely — January is in the dry Harmattan season)
> ✏️ **Practice:** Exercise 15.1, at the end of section 15.2, covers this section too. Tap **Quick check** to try its questions.

pages.title: Outcomes of experiments
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Classify the likelihood of a single outcome occurring in a probability experiment as impossible, possible or certain.
Curriculum indicator B7.4.2.1.2
> 🔑 **Key idea: Experiment, outcome and sample space** — A **probability experiment** is an action whose result is uncertain, such as tossing a coin or throwing a die. Each possible result is an **outcome**. The list of all possible outcomes is the **sample space**. An **event** is one outcome or a group of outcomes.
| **Experiment** | **Sample space** | **Number of outcomes** |
|---|---|---|
| Tossing a coin | {Head, Tail} | 2 |
| Throwing a die | {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} | 6 |
| Spinning a 4-colour spinner | {red, blue, green, yellow} | 4 |
## ✏️ Example 15.3
A fair die is thrown once. Describe each outcome as impossible, possible or certain.
A. Obtaining the number 1 B. Obtaining the number 7 C. Obtaining the number 4 D. Obtaining a number less than 7
**Solution**
A. **possible** B. **impossible** (7 is not in the sample space) C. **possible** D. **certain**
## ✏️ Example 15.4
Two dice are thrown and the numbers are added. Describe each outcome.
A. A total of 12 B. A total of 2 C. A total of 13 D. A total of 7
**Solution**
[[fig:m7-f75]]
Figure 15.2: Totals when two dice are thrown
A. **possible** (only 6 + 6; unlikely) B. **possible** (only 1 + 1; unlikely) C. **impossible** (the largest total is 12) D. **possible** (the most likely total: 6 ways out of 36)

pages.title: Calculating probability
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Calculate the probability of the event and express the probability as fractions, decimals, percentages and/or ratios.
Curriculum indicator B7.4.2.1.3
> 🔑 **Key idea: Probability** — When all outcomes are **equally likely** (e.g. a fair die), the probability of an event E is:
P(E) = [[number of favourable outcomes/total number of possible outcomes]]
Probability can be written as a fraction, a decimal, a percentage or a ratio (favourable : total). It always lies between 0 and 1.
## ✏️ Example 15.5
A fair die is rolled once. Find the probability of rolling each event. Express each probability as a fraction, decimal, percentage and ratio.
**Solution**
Sample space: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, so there are 6 equally likely outcomes.
| **The probability of rolling …** | **Favourable outcomes** | **Fraction** | **Decimal** | **Percentage** | **Ratio** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. a factor of 60 | 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 | [[6/6]] = 1 | 1 | 100% | 6 : 6 = 1 : 1 |
| 2. a multiple of 3 | 3, 6 | [[2/6]] = [[1/3]] | 0.33 | 33[[1/3]]% | 1 : 3 |
| 3. a factor of 2 | 1, 2 | [[1/3]] | 0.33 | 33[[1/3]]% | 1 : 3 |
| 4. a divisor of 12 | 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 | [[5/6]] | 0.83 | 83[[1/3]]% | 5 : 6 |
| 5. a 3 or greater | 3, 4, 5, 6 | [[4/6]] = [[2/3]] | 0.67 | 66[[2/3]]% | 2 : 3 |
| 6. a factor of 8 | 1, 2, 4 | [[3/6]] = [[1/2]] | 0.5 | 50% | 1 : 2 |
| 7. a factor of 6 | 1, 2, 3, 6 | [[2/3]] | 0.67 | 66[[2/3]]% | 2 : 3 |
| 8. a divisor of 30 | 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 | [[5/6]] | 0.83 | 83[[1/3]]% | 5 : 6 |
| 9. a 3 or smaller | 1, 2, 3 | [[1/2]] | 0.5 | 50% | 1 : 2 |
(Decimals are rounded to 2 decimal places. The ratio here compares favourable outcomes to all outcomes.)

pages.title: Example 15.6
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 15.6
A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green bottle tops. One is picked at random. Find the probability that it is a) red b) blue c) not green d) yellow.
**Solution**
Total = 5 + 3 + 2 = 10.
a) P(red) = [[5/10]] = [[1/2]] = 0.5 = 50%
b) P(blue) = [[3/10]] = 0.3 = 30%
c) P(not green) = [[8/10]] = [[4/5]] = 0.8 = 80%
d) P(yellow) = [[0/10]] = **0** (impossible)
> ✨ **Did you know?** P(event does not happen) = 1 − P(event happens). For example, P(not green) = 1 − [[2/10]] = [[8/10]].
> 🧪 **Activity 15.1 — Experimental probability**
In pairs, toss a coin 50 times and record the number of heads. Calculate [[number of heads/50]]. Combine the results of the whole class. Is the class result close to [[1/2]]? Discuss why results from more tosses are usually closer to the theoretical probability.

pages.title: Exercise 15.2
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 15.2** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. A letter is chosen at random from the word MATHEMATICS. Find the probability that it is: a) M b) a vowel c) T or S d) Z
2. A spinner has 8 equal sectors numbered 1 to 8. Find the probability of spinning: a) an even number b) a prime number c) a number greater than 6 d) a multiple of 4. Give each answer as a fraction, decimal and percentage.
3. A box contains 12 pens: 4 black, 5 blue and 3 red. One pen is taken at random. Find P(blue), P(not black) and P(black or red).
4. The probability that it will rain tomorrow is 0.35. What is the probability that it will not rain?
5. A class has 18 boys and 22 girls. A learner is chosen at random to be class prefect. Find the probability that a girl is chosen, as a percentage.

pages.title: Chapter 15 summary
pages.body:
- Impossible = 0, certain = 1, possible = between 0 and 1.
- The sample space lists all possible outcomes.
- P(E) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes (for equally likely outcomes).
- P(not E) = 1 − P(E).
